opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a pretty consistent thread if you look at what they've published.

Going back to GPT-3, the paper says they used alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention patterns, similar to the Sparse Transformer. That came out of OpenAI's own Sparse Transformer work from 2019, where Rewon Child and others were thinking hard about how to avoid paying the full quadratic cost at every layer. So the idea that not every layer needs to see the whole context has been part of their thinking for a long time.

Then with gpt-oss, the open-weight models from 2025, you see it very explicitly: they interleave full-attention layers with sliding-window layers that use a very small window, around 128 tokens. They also add attention sinks, learned per-head bias terms that let the model put attention mass somewhere harmless. With a short window, that matters a lot for stability, because the softmax has to put its probability mass somewhere even when nothing in the local window is relevant.

My reading is that this is a very pragmatic, engineering-driven choice. Most of what a layer does is local: syntax, nearby token dependencies, local copying. You don't need a global KV cache for that. So you make most layers cheap and keep a few global layers to handle long-range retrieval. The KV cache shrinks a lot, which is what really dominates inference cost at long context, and you lose surprisingly little quality.

From my perspective working on linear attention and efficient sequence models, this is also a sign of where the field converged. People used to frame it as a binary: full attention or some efficient replacement. In practice the frontier labs are doing hybrids. Google's Gemma models mix local and global attention layers, and Character.AI described something similar. Some Chinese labs are hybridizing linear attention with full attention. Sliding window is the simplest, most hardware-friendly version of the hybrid idea. It's easy to implement and it plays well with existing kernels.

The interesting research question is whether sliding window is the right "cheap" component. A sliding window just forgets everything outside the window. Linear attention or state-space-style layers compress the distant past into a fixed-size state instead of dropping it. So one way to see the hybrid design space is: what do you put in the cheap layers, a hard local window or a learned recurrent memory? I think that's still open. OpenAI's choice suggests that if you have enough global layers, plain local attention is good enough, but I don't think that's the final answer, especially as contexts get longer and agentic workloads get heavier.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-3 used alternating dense and locally banded sparse attention, communicating a mix of global and local attention.

r002.rationale: It calls this a consistent thread and describes sliding-window layers in gpt-oss, implying OpenAI continued the approach after GPT-3.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think OpenAI's use of sliding-window attention is one of those things that people underrate because it looks like a "boring" engineering choice, but it actually tells you a lot about how they think about the tradeoff between modeling quality and systems efficiency.

If you go back to GPT-3, the paper already mentions that they alternate dense and locally banded sparse attention patterns in the layers, which is basically the Sparse Transformer idea from Rewon Child and others at OpenAI in 2019. So the lineage is quite old. The intuition is simple: most tokens really only need to attend to their recent context most of the time, and a small number of layers or heads with full attention are enough to carry the long-range information. If you interleave local and global layers, you cut the KV cache and the attention FLOPs a lot, and you lose surprisingly little.

Then when they open-sourced gpt-oss last year, you could actually see it concretely: alternating layers of banded, sliding-window attention with a window of 128 tokens and full attention, plus attention sinks. That confirmed what a lot of us suspected from the earlier papers and from hints about their production models. The attention sink part is interesting too, because it is a learned per-head bias that lets the softmax "put mass nowhere," which stabilizes long-context behavior with local attention. That connects nicely to the StreamingLLM observation about sink tokens.

From my perspective, coming from the linear attention and state-space side, I read this as OpenAI being pragmatic. Sliding-window attention is the cheapest possible form of "bounded memory" attention. It is just a hardware-friendly truncation of softmax attention, and FlashAttention supports it almost for free, so you get the efficiency gains without touching the kernel stack much. Linear attention or something like Mamba gives you a different kind of bounded memory, a compressed state rather than a hard cutoff, and I would argue that for many tasks a learned compressed state is a better inductive bias than simply forgetting everything beyond 128 tokens. But the hybrid architecture logic is the same: use a cheap, local or recurrent mechanism for most layers, keep a few full attention layers for precise retrieval.

So I see the whole industry converging on this hybrid design space. OpenAI picked sliding window as their cheap component, Google's Gemma did something similar, while others, like what we did with Gated DeltaNet in Qwen3-Next or what NVIDIA did with Nemotron-H, picked linear attention or SSMs as the cheap component. The interesting research question now is not "local versus global," but which cheap mechanism gives you the best quality per unit of memory and compute, and how many global layers you really need. My bet is that the recurrent, state-based mechanisms will win in the long run, because they can learn what to keep instead of being forced to drop it, but OpenAI's history shows that even the simplest version of this idea gets you most of the way there.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-3 alternated dense attention with locally banded sparse attention, then describes these as interleaved local and global layers.

r002.rationale: It connects the GPT-3 approach to hints about OpenAI’s production models and says the later gpt-oss release confirmed that pattern, implying continued use.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about assuming there’s a documented history of OpenAI using sliding-window attention. That’s a specific architectural choice: each token attends to a limited neighborhood of earlier tokens rather than the entire preceding context. It can reduce computation, but access to distant information then depends on other parts of the architecture.

It’s also different from truncating a conversation to fit a context window. From the information we have here, I can explain that distinction, but I can’t establish which OpenAI models used sliding-window attention or when. Is there a particular model or paper you’re referring to?

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between OpenAI experimenting with local attention and OpenAI consistently using sliding-window attention in its production models. Those are different claims.

Sliding-window attention lets each token attend to a nearby stretch of tokens instead of the entire preceding context. That can reduce computation, but it also limits direct access to information farther away unless you combine it with other attention patterns.

From the conversation so far, we don’t have evidence establishing which OpenAI models used it or when. So I wouldn’t give you a confident historical timeline. I’d want to ground that discussion in specific architecture disclosures and distinguish a purely sliding window from a hybrid of local and global attention.
